packs.title: Islands & Inventions
packs.promise: Find small clues, everyday inventions and changing views across Stockholm’s islands.

q.s: Collect details that make a large building readable.
st: From an open public pavement on Slottsbacken, choose one visible entrance or doorway without approaching guards or barriers.
Collect three details by looking: a large outline, a medium repeating element and a small decoration. Describe or sketch them without touching.
Decide which detail helps you recognise the entrance from farther away. Test that idea by changing your view a few safe paces, or by reducing a photograph on your screen.
Arrange the three details from most useful at a distance to most useful close up. There is no official right ranking.

q.s: Connect everyday objects to the lives around them.
st: Choose three accessible labeled objects in Nordic Life, or in its official online images and texts. Look for one that relates to warmth, one to work and one to celebration; a different everyday need may replace a missing category.
Use each label or exhibition text to record what the object was for. Do not infer someone’s identity or a whole culture from appearance.
Connect two objects that respond differently to a similar need. Identify one visible difference and one source-supported difference.
Choose which question you would ask about their makers or users. Keep it a question if the display does not answer it.

q.s: Collect a meal idea through contrasting textures.
st: Look for three visibly displayed ingredients or foods with different textures: perhaps crisp-looking, smooth and leafy. Choose what suits your own food preferences.
Invent a meal that could bring them together. Describe what each contributes, without assuming ingredients, allergens or preparation from appearance.
Replace one choice with a different visible option. Decide how that changes the imagined meal. Labels or the trader’s published description may supply facts; guessing is unnecessary.

packs.title: Södermalm in Layers
packs.promise: Explore Södermalm through tiny compositions, street-level clues and unhurried hilltop paths.

q.s: Give everyday things a place in an imagined room.
st: Choose three labeled everyday objects or room details in an accessible part of the Stockholm exhibition. Include different purposes, such as cooking, working or resting.
Record each purpose from the display text, then place the three in an imaginary small room. Your arrangement is a design idea, not a reconstruction of someone’s home.
Decide which two things need to be close together and which should be separated. Give one practical reason for each choice.

q.s: Make a tiny diptych by removing one layer.
st: Choose a safe stationary view with something near you, water in the middle and a distant shore. If fog hides a layer, use the official photograph.
Make three simple horizontal bands in a sketch or describe what belongs in each. This is a composition, not a map or building-identification quiz.
Make a second version with one layer removed or given more space. Compare which version feels more open and which feels closer.

q.s: Curate a miniature exhibition through the windows.
st: Choose two visible display works or objects that share a colour, shape or arrangement. Describe the connection using only what you can see.
Give that pair an invented exhibition theme of a few words. It is your grouping, not a claim about the artists’ intentions.
Find a third visible thing that breaks your rule. Decide whether to include it as a deliberate surprise or leave it out, and explain why.
